To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the light adaptation of rod photoreceptors in the dark-adapted state involves a decrease in the gain of the transduction cascade and an increase in the rate of recovery of the dark state, and that the gain decrease and recovery-rate increase are mediated by different mechanisms.

the light-activated and spontaneous activities of rod phototransducing cells in mouse retinas can be described quantitatively with a single model, and that the model can be used to explain the effects of genetic mutations on these activities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of light adaptation in rod phototransductions.
the role of Ca2+ in the modulation of rod phototransductive signaling.
understanding how the visual system adapts to different levels of illumination, and the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie this adaptation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GCAPs are not involved in light adaptation in rods.
the model of Hamer et. al. (2005) can be used to describe and explain most, but not all, of the experimental data on rod light adaptation presented in this paper.
the GCAPs play a significant role in the adaptation process, but the exact mechanism of their action is not yet fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the model of Hamer et. al., is the best model for rod photoreception.
the GCAP1/3 proteins are the major modulator of the PDE6* lifetime.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the modulation of the PDE6* decay rate is the key to understanding the mechanism of the modulation of the light sensitivity of rods.
the GCAPs are the key modulator of the rate of the decay of activated phosphodiestesterase.
